name: Albarello apothecary ware
region: Florence, Faenza, Deruta and Venice, Italy; then Spain and the Low Countries
summary: Tin-glazed earthenware jars and jugs that Italian potters made for the shelf of the pharmacy. The waisted albarello holds dry drugs, and the label names the drug in a painted cartouche.

philosophy.core_thesis: A drug jar must tell a clerk which drug it holds, so the label is part of the pot: a painted cartouche on a clean white tin glaze.
design_principles: Throw a waisted cylinder with a flared lip and foot, so that a hand holds it and a cord ties on a parchment lid.
Make the height 15 to 30 cm and the width a little more than half of the height.
Cover the whole pot with an opaque white tin glaze about 0.5 mm thick.
Paint a cartouche or a scroll on the front, and write the name of the drug in it in Latin.
Paint blue on the raw glaze with cobalt; add manganese purple, copper green and ochre in polychrome work.
Paint a foliage ground, the "oak-leaf" or "peacock-feather" pattern, round the label.
Give a syrup jar a spout and a strap handle, and a bottle a long neck with a flat mouth.
anti_patterns: A body that is not covered by white glaze
Modern lettering in a sans-serif face
A narrow cylinder with no waist
A glaze that crackles in a printed net
Heavy gold or lustre over the whole pot

form.shape: Albarelli (waisted drug jars), spouted syrup jars, bottles with a long neck and ewers, all made as sets for one pharmacy.
form.profile: A cylinder with a concave waist, a shoulder that rises to a short neck and a flared lip that ties on a lid.
form.foot_and_rim: A flat or slightly splayed foot; the rim is a small bead under which a cord ties on the lid of parchment or leather.
form.proportion: Height 15 to 30 cm; the wall is 4 to 8 mm thick; the waist is about 70 % of the width at the shoulder.
rules: Waist the jar so that fingers hold it and so that jars stand in rows.
Keep one label zone on the front, 6 to 10 cm wide.
Make a set in one height, so that the shelf looks orderly.

bodies.rule: Use a buff or pink earthenware that fires soft at about 1000 °C and takes a thick tin glaze. A hard body does not suit it: the glaze must grip a porous clay.

methods: turning the shoulder and foot when leather-hard
forming.joins: Spouts and handles are luted with slip on the leather-hard body; the lip is turned to take a cord.
forming.details: Thin glaze at the rim, a ring of three stilt marks inside the foot, and a slight blur of blue where the colour sank into the glaze.

glaze.pattern: A cartouche or a ribbon with the name of the drug, set in a ground of oak leaves, foliage, peacock-feather scales or grotesques; some jars show a portrait or a saint.
glaze.gloss: A smooth, deep gloss of about 55 to 80 GU, softer on the inside.
glaze.wear: The tin glaze chips at the lip and the foot and shows the buff body; the painted colour stays fresh.

palette.strategy: Cobalt blue on milk-white; polychrome jars add manganese purple, copper green and antimony yellow.

firing.kiln: A wood-fired updraught kiln; one firing for the biscuit and one for the glaze.
processes: lustre firing in a muffle kiln, for lustred jars only
firing.scale: Pharmacies ordered sets of 50 to 300 jars; Faenza, Deruta and Venice shipped them to hospitals and convents across Europe.
firing.signs: A painted cartouche with a Latin drug name, stilt marks in the foot ring, and a bead under the lip.

Bottle with a long neck for oils and a lustre label

positive: painted cartouche with a Latin drug name
still-life museum photograph, soft north light

Albarello with a portrait of a woman

emotion.target_response: A tidy, learned calm: the viewer sees rows of white jars with blue labels and thinks of a clean, ordered shop.

use_cases: a set dressing for a pharmacy or a still life of the Renaissance
a museum label on Italian maiolica
a kitchen jar set that borrows the albarello waist
avoid_when: the brief needs stoneware or salt glaze
the brief needs a modern lidded canister

modifiers.how: Change the body to stoneware and the glaze to salt; replace the label with a relief mask.
Change to a red earthenware with a clear lead glaze and trail the pattern in cream slip.
